newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa business seeks talks to avert new strike.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa business seeks talks to avert new strike.

text.p: South African business called on Wednesday for high level talks with labour and government to head off the threat of further damaging strike action, following a one-day stoppage over labour legislation on Monday.
"Negotiations cannot be held hostage by arbitrary deadlines," Business South Africa (BSA) deputy president Leslie Boyd told a news briefing.

He was referring to the Congress of South African Trade Unions' 14-day ultimatum to business this week to present revised proposals on the controversial Basic Conditions of Employment Bill or face further strike action.
"We propose a set of meetings at the highest level between government, labour and business to seek a way forward," Boyd said.

These talks could take place either within the established National Economic Development and Labour Council (Nedlac), where talks with a view to settlement over the bill have taken place, or in a separate forum.

Cosatu said two million workers had responded to the 24-hour strike call on Monday while business said support for the strike -- the third national stoppage since the 1994 elections -- had proved limited.
Adrian du Plessis, BSA negotiator at Nedlac, said it was vital that the various parties found consensus on outstanding issues.
"The differences between the parties are deep but at the highest level it seems there are common objectives in areas such as job creation, growth and labour market fairness," du Plessis said.
Government, labour and business were united by a broad set of common objectives and needed to find a way to translate these into legislation.
"We have to find consensus on the critical issue of labour market policy...around this specific law we need consensus otherwise it won't work," du Plessis said.
The employment bill, approved by cabinet in April, sets a 45-hour working week and four months' maternity leave.
Cosatu, which represents 1.9 million members, wants a 40-hour week phased in within five years, six months' maternity leave and the minimum age for formal employment to be set at 18.
It is also opposed to the right of employers to apply for variations of, or exemptions from, the minimum standards set out in the bill.
Business is concerned that the bill will increase its costs.

It strongly disagrees with, among others, proposals for a reduction in the working week to 40 hours, a reduction in the overtime rate from time-and-a-third to time-and-a-half and provisions for three days' paid family responsibility leave.
